Startup roadmap

A startup is not just a small company or a clever app. It is a team searching for a repeatable way to solve a meaningful problem—and a sustainable way to deliver that solution.

01 · Problem

Find a real struggle

Start with a specific person, a repeated frustration, and the cost of leaving it unsolved.

02 · Evidence

Replace guesses with learning

Talk to people, study current workarounds, and look for behavior—not polite compliments.

03 · Experiment

Test the smallest promise

Use a prototype, landing page, pilot, or manual service before building the full product.

Right nowWrite down one repeated problem you have personally observed.

Do not choose a solution yet. Name the person, moment, workaround, and cost.

Startup academy

Work through the parts of a startup in any order. Open a lesson, use its template, and mark it complete. Your progress and workspace answers stay in this browser.

Your learning progress0 of 24 lessons complete
Track 01

Turn an observation into a clear business idea

Define the problem, the person, and the value before choosing features.

Lesson 01Problem statement+

A useful problem statement names a specific customer, a situation, the job they are trying to do, the obstacle, and the cost of the problem. It should describe the problem without quietly prescribing your favorite solution.

Template

[Customer] struggles to [make progress] when [situation] because [root cause], causing [time, money, risk, or frustration].

  • Weak: “Students need a better food app.”
  • Stronger: “Students with evening labs struggle to find an affordable campus meal after 8 p.m., leading them to skip dinner or pay delivery fees.”
Lesson 02Customer segment and profile+

A segment is a group whose needs, behavior, and buying situation are similar enough for one focused strategy. “Everyone” is not a usable first segment.

Demographics

Age, income, education, role, organization size, or life stage.

Geographics

Country, region, campus, neighborhood, climate, or remote/in-person context.

Psychographics

Values, motivations, identity, attitudes, priorities, and risk tolerance.

Behavior

Frequency, trigger, current workaround, purchase process, and willingness to switch.

Customer profile

Our early adopter is [specific person] who experiences [trigger/problem] [frequency], currently uses [alternative], and cares most about [desired outcome].

Lesson 03Target market and beachhead+

Your target market is the segment you intentionally serve. Your beachhead is the smallest group you can reach, satisfy, and learn from first. Prioritize segments by problem intensity, reachability, ability to pay, urgency, and strategic fit.

Decision test

If you had only two weeks and $100, which customer group could you contact directly and offer a credible test to?

Lesson 04Unique value proposition (UVP)+

A UVP explains the important outcome, the intended customer, and why your approach is meaningfully better than the current alternative. It is not a slogan.

UVP statement

For [target customer] who needs [job/outcome], [product] is a [category] that [primary benefit]. Unlike [alternative], it [credible difference].

Sustainable goals: decide whether environmental or social impact is part of the customer value, an operating constraint, or a measurable mission. Name the metric—such as waste avoided, access improved, or emissions reduced—rather than using vague “green” claims.

Lesson 05Elevator pitch+

A strong 30–60 second pitch creates interest, not information overload. Lead with the customer and problem, explain the outcome, show one reason to believe, and end with a specific ask.

  1. Hook: a concrete problem or surprising observation.
  2. Who + problem: the target user and costly moment.
  3. Solution + benefit: what changes for them.
  4. Proof: interviews, pilot results, traction, or relevant insight.
  5. Ask: an introduction, interview, pilot, feedback, or funding conversation.

Track 02

Test behavior before building too much

Use interviews and small experiments to replace opinions with evidence.

Lesson 06Features and benefits+

A feature is what the product does. A benefit is the useful change a customer experiences. Connect every feature to the problem, outcome, and evidence needed.

FeatureBenefitProof metric
One-click event filterLess searchingTime to find an event
Deadline remindersFewer missed tasksOn-time completion rate

Prioritize with must-have, should-have, could-have, not-now. A top feature directly solves the primary problem; an impressive feature that does not is still a distraction.

Lesson 07Minimum viable product+

An MVP is the smallest experience that tests your riskiest business assumption while still delivering enough value for a real response. It may be a landing page, concierge service, spreadsheet, preorder, clickable prototype, or limited pilot.

MVP test

We need to learn whether [customer] will [meaningful behavior] for [outcome]. We can test this with [small experience] and will continue if [threshold].

Lesson 08Customer interviews+

Interview people who recently experienced the problem. Ask about specific past events, not imagined future behavior. Do not pitch during a problem interview.

  • “Tell me about the last time this happened.”
  • “What did you do next?”
  • “What was hardest, slowest, or most expensive?”
  • “What have you already tried?”
  • “Who decides or pays?”

Write exact quotes, behaviors, workarounds, frequency, and contradictions. Five interviews can reveal patterns; they do not prove an entire market.

Lesson 09Solution interviews and usability+

After the problem is understood, show a low-fidelity solution. Give the participant a realistic task and ask them to think aloud. Watch where they hesitate instead of teaching them how it works.

End with a meaningful commitment: join a pilot, schedule a follow-up, share data, introduce a buyer, preorder, or pay. Compliments are not validation.

Lesson 10Marketing tests and survey results+

A useful experiment has one hypothesis, one audience, one offer, one primary metric, a time limit, and a decision rule set before launch. Examples include two landing-page messages, waitlist conversion, outreach replies, a small paid-ad test, or two price points.

Surveys are strongest for measuring patterns after interviews help you write good questions. Report sample source, sample size, question wording, response distribution, missing responses, and limitations. Avoid treating a convenience sample as the whole market.

Track 03

Understand the market and the alternatives

Size the opportunity, study competition, and test feasibility.

Lesson 11Market sizing: TAM, SAM, SOM+
TAM

Total annual demand if every relevant buyer used your solution.

SAM

The portion you can serve with your product, geography, channel, and constraints.

SOM

The realistic share you could capture in a defined period with available resources.

Use both top-down sources and a bottom-up model: reachable accounts × realistic annual revenue per account. State every assumption and never present TAM as a sales forecast.

Lesson 12Competitive analysis+

Competition includes direct products, indirect approaches, do-it-yourself workarounds, and doing nothing. Compare the customer segment, job solved, pricing, channel, strengths, weaknesses, switching costs, and proof—not just feature counts.

Use the analysis to find an underserved need or a different tradeoff. “We have no competitors” usually means the current workaround has not been identified.

Official SBA market-research guide ↗

Lesson 13SWOT and feasibility+

Strengths and weaknesses are internal. Opportunities and threats are external. Convert the list into action: use a strength to pursue an opportunity, correct a weakness, and reduce exposure to a threat.

Feasibility asks whether the venture is desirable to customers, technically and operationally possible, legally responsible, and financially sustainable. Identify the assumption that could break the idea first.

Track 04

Make the right promise in the right place

Connect brand, channels, content, and a trustworthy website.

Lesson 14Branding+

A brand is the expectation people build from every interaction. Define your audience, positioning, personality, promise, reasons to believe, voice, visual system, and consistency rules. A logo supports the brand; it is not the whole brand.

Before committing to a name, check domain availability, social handles, state business records, and similar trademarks. Test whether the name is pronounceable, memorable, and appropriate across likely markets.

Lesson 15Marketing plan, mix, and functions+

The classic marketing mix is Product, Price, Place, and Promotion. Services often add People, Process, and Physical evidence. Make the choices reinforce one position.

Research

Segments, needs, competitors, trends, and demand.

Offer

Product design, benefits, brand, packaging, and pricing.

Go to market

Distribution, promotion, sales, service, and retention.

A one-page plan should name the objective, audience, insight, message, offer, channels, budget, calendar, owner, primary metric, and review date.

Lesson 16Social media and advertising+

Choose channels based on where the customer already pays attention and how they make the purchase—not which platform is newest. Build content around customer questions, useful proof, demonstrations, stories, and calls to action.

For paid tests, define audience, creative, offer, landing page, budget cap, and one conversion metric. Track impressions → clicks → qualified actions → customers. Advertising claims must be truthful, supported, and not misleading; disclose material connections with endorsers clearly.

Official FTC advertising guidance ↗

Lesson 17Website and domain—from zero to launch+
  1. Choose the job: validation landing page, portfolio, booking site, store, community, or product app.
  2. Pick a name and domain: choose a short, readable domain through an accredited registrar. You rent registration by the year; enable auto-renew, account MFA, registrar lock, and accurate contact information.
  3. Choose a platform: a hosted builder is fastest; a CMS offers content flexibility; static HTML/GitHub Pages is inexpensive for informational sites; a web application needs hosting, a database, authentication, and maintenance.
  4. Connect DNS: the registrar manages ownership; DNS records point the domain to hosting. Common records include A/AAAA, CNAME, MX for email, and TXT for verification/security.
  5. Design the core journey: one clear audience, headline/UVP, benefits and proof, strong call to action, contact details, and only the pages users need.
  6. Make it trustworthy: HTTPS, mobile layout, accessible contrast and labels, fast images, working forms, privacy notice, terms when appropriate, refund/shipping policies for commerce, and truthful claims.
  7. Measure: analytics with consent where required, search-console verification, conversion events, uptime, and form testing. Collect only data you need.
  8. Maintain: renew domain and hosting, update software, back up content, patch security issues, test links/forms, and keep owner access documented.

Minimum pages: Home, Product/Service, About or credibility, Contact, and required policy pages. Add FAQ, pricing, case studies, or a blog only when they support a customer decision.

SEO basics: useful page titles, one clear topic per page, descriptive URLs, headings that match questions, original helpful content, alt text, internal links, sitemap, and performance. SEO cannot rescue a page that gives visitors no value.

Track 05

Build an economic model, not just a price

Understand revenue, direct costs, cash, projections, and possible exits.

Lesson 18Revenue models+

Common models include one-time sales, subscription, usage-based, transaction fee, marketplace commission, licensing, advertising, sponsorship, freemium, services, leasing, and franchising. Choose based on how value is delivered and how customers prefer to buy.

Test the unit: who pays, for what, how often, through which contract or checkout, and what causes expansion or cancellation. Mixing models too early makes learning harder.

Lesson 19COGS, margin, and pricing strategy+

COGS includes direct costs required to deliver one unit: materials, production labor, packaging, transaction fees, shipping subsidy, or usage-based infrastructure. Gross profit = revenue − COGS; gross margin % = gross profit ÷ revenue.

Pricing approaches include cost-plus, competitor-based, value-based, tiered, penetration, skimming, bundle, subscription, and usage-based. Use costs as a floor, customer value and alternatives as context, then test willingness to pay. Include discounts, returns, taxes, channel fees, and support in the model.

Interactive tool

Price and unit-economics check

See whether a price covers direct cost and contributes toward overhead.

Gross margin68.0%
Contribution$1,700
Break-even units59
Lesson 20Financial model and banking+

A useful model connects assumptions to monthly revenue, COGS, payroll, operating expenses, cash flow, and cash balance. Build a base case plus conservative and upside scenarios. Track actuals against the model and update assumptions rather than hiding misses.

Core statements serve different jobs: the income statement shows performance over time, the cash-flow statement explains cash movement, and the balance sheet shows assets, liabilities, and equity at a point in time.

Before accepting or spending business money, choose the entity and tax setup, obtain required registrations/EIN, then compare business accounts by fees, transaction limits, deposit insurance, payment tools, integrations, and signer controls. Keep business and personal activity separate and reconcile monthly.

IRS starting and recordkeeping guidance ↗

Lesson 21Funding and exit strategies+

Funding may come from revenue/bootstrapping, grants, competitions, friends and family, crowdfunding, debt, angels, venture capital, or strategic partners. Match the source to risk, repayment ability, growth expectations, ownership tradeoffs, and use of funds.

Possible exits include owner operation, family or employee succession, acquisition, merger, management buyout, licensing assets, public offering for rare high-growth firms, or orderly closure. Plan clean records, transferable contracts, documented IP, governance, and reduced dependence on one founder long before an exit.

Official SBA exit guidance ↗

Track 06

Protect the company, founders, customers, and work

This U.S.-focused overview is a decision checklist—not personal legal or tax advice.

Lesson 22Structures, founders, and partnerships+

Common U.S. forms include sole proprietorship, general or limited partnership, LLP, LLC, and corporation. The choice changes liability, taxes, governance, fundraising, filing, and administration. Rules vary by state and situation.

“Partnership” can also describe a working relationship: co-marketing, referral/affiliate, distribution, supplier, licensing, joint venture, strategic alliance, or equity partnership. Put scope, ownership, money, confidentiality, performance, brand use, liability, data, termination, and dispute terms in writing.

Founder agreements should address roles, decision rights, equity, vesting, IP assignment, time commitment, compensation, fundraising, departures, deadlock, and what happens if someone stops contributing.

Compare structures at SBA.gov ↗

Lesson 23Trademarks, patents, NDAs, and attorneys+
Trademark

Protects source-identifying names, logos, and related brand elements for goods/services.

Patent

May protect a qualifying new invention; it gives exclusion rights, not automatic permission to practice it.

Copyright

Protects original expression such as writing, art, code, photos, or video—not the underlying idea.

Trade secret

Protects valuable confidential information when reasonable secrecy measures are maintained.

Search before adopting a brand or filing. Patent timing can matter, and public disclosure may affect rights. NDAs can define confidential information, permitted use, exclusions, duration, return/destruction, and remedies, but they do not replace access controls, IP assignment, or a well-scoped contract.

Talk to an attorney when founder equity or ownership is unclear, a regulated product is involved, meaningful contracts or hiring begin, IP is core to the venture, investors are approaching, a dispute or demand arrives, or the cost of being wrong is high. For patents, consider a USPTO-registered patent attorney or agent.

USPTO trademark basics ↗USPTO patent essentials ↗
Lesson 24Legal and financial launch checklist+
Form and register
  • Choose entity, state, business name, and ownership
  • Register assumed names where required
  • Obtain EIN/tax IDs and licenses/permits
  • Document governance and founder approvals
Operate responsibly
  • Separate bank account, bookkeeping, taxes, and records
  • Written customer, vendor, contractor, and employee terms
  • Insurance appropriate to product and risk
  • Privacy, cybersecurity, accessibility, and data retention
Protect assets
  • IP ownership and assignments from every contributor
  • Trademark/domain clearance and renewal calendar
  • Confidentiality and restricted access
  • Contract, compliance, and corporate-record storage

Requirements depend on location, industry, workforce, customers, and data. Recheck federal, state, local, and industry rules before launch and as the business changes.

SBA launch checklist ↗IRS starting-a-business guide ↗
Track 07

Turn the evidence into a decision

Finish with a business case that makes assumptions and limitations visible.

01

Summary of key points

Restate the customer, problem, UVP, solution, market, model, evidence, economics, risks, and next milestone in plain language.

02

Feasibility

Rate desirability, technical delivery, operations, legal responsibility, and financial viability. Name what still needs proof.

03

SWOT

Translate the four boxes into actions, owners, evidence, and review dates instead of ending with a list.

04

Competitive analysis

Explain the current alternatives, your focused advantage, switching barriers, and how competitors may respond.

05

Survey and interview results

Report method, sample, exact measures, findings, contradictions, bias, and what the evidence does—and does not—support.

06

Conclusion and next test

Choose continue, revise, pause, or stop. Define the next assumption, test, threshold, budget, owner, and decision date.

Final recommendation

Based on [evidence], we recommend [decision] because [reason]. The largest remaining risk is [assumption], which we will test by [experiment] before [date].

Problem to solution

Problem statement

Make the problem narrow enough to test

[Specific user] struggles to [make progress] when [situation] because [root cause], which leads to [measurable cost].

“Students need a productivity app” is broad. “First-year commuters miss campus events because information is scattered across five channels” is testable.

Solution hypothesis

Describe an outcome, not a feature pile

We believe [solution] will help [user] achieve [outcome]. We will know when [behavior or metric] changes.

Your first solution is a hypothesis. Learning that it is wrong early is progress, not failure.

Quick problem check

Ideas and brainstorming

Strong startup ideas usually come from close observation: inconvenient workflows, excluded users, expensive delays, new technology, or a process you understand unusually well.

Observe

Keep a friction log

Record repeated complaints, awkward workarounds, waiting, waste, and tasks people avoid.

Reframe

Ask “How might we?”

Turn a complaint into an open challenge without deciding the answer too early.

Expand

Create 20 options

Separate idea generation from judgment. Include manual, service, software, and community solutions.

Narrow

Score the evidence

Rank urgency, access to users, willingness to act, testability, and your unfair insight.

15-minute idea sprint

Choose one community you know. List five repeated problems, three current workarounds for each, and one way to test demand this week for the strongest problem.

Validation and MVP

Customer discovery

Interview the past, not the imaginary future

  • “Tell me about the last time this happened.”
  • “What did you do instead?”
  • “What did that cost in time, money, or stress?”
  • “Who decides whether to try or buy a solution?”

Avoid pitching during discovery. The goal is to understand behavior and decision-making.

Minimum viable product

Build the smallest credible test

  • Clickable prototype for usability
  • Landing page or waitlist for demand
  • Manual concierge service for delivery
  • Paid pilot or preorder for willingness to pay

An MVP is a learning instrument. Choose it based on the riskiest assumption—not the most exciting feature.

Evidence before scaleThe NSF I-Corps program uses experiential customer discovery to reduce commercialization risk.

Legal basics

Educational guidance, not legal advice. Requirements depend on your country, state, industry, team, and customers. Use official sources and consult a qualified attorney or accountant for decisions with legal or tax consequences.
Founders

Put agreements in writing

Clarify roles, ownership, vesting, decision rights, departures, and who owns work created for the startup.

Entity

Choose structure deliberately

Structure affects taxes, liability, paperwork, fundraising, and ownership. Do not copy another startup blindly.

SBA structure guide ↗
Identity

Check names and IP

A domain or social handle does not establish trademark rights. Search similar marks and understand what your brand identifies.

USPTO trademark basics ↗
Registration

Register in the right order

Check state or local formation, licenses, permits, tax registration, and banking requirements. In the U.S., form an entity before requesting its EIN.

IRS EIN guidance ↗
Data

Protect customer information

Collect only what you need, secure access, explain usage clearly, and review rules for minors, health, education, payments, and location data.

People

Know who works for you

Employee and contractor classifications have different tax, wage, benefit, and IP consequences.

Financial foundations

You do not need an MBA to understand startup finance. You do need a clear view of cash, costs, price, unit economics, and how long you can keep learning.

Costs

Separate one-time and monthly costs

Include software, equipment, licenses, insurance, contractors, marketing, payment fees, and a realistic buffer.

Price

Connect price to value

Test willingness to pay. Revenue is stronger evidence than sign-ups, and margin matters more than revenue alone.

Cash

Track burn and runway

Net burn is monthly cash out minus cash in. Runway estimates how many months remain at the current burn.

Funding

Match money to the milestone

Bootstrapping, grants, competitions, loans, and equity each change risk, control, and expectations.

Build a realistic cost mapThe SBA recommends identifying one-time and monthly expenses before launch, then using them for profit, break-even, and funding estimates.

What can you responsibly estimate?

With consistent historical data, models can estimate retention risk, demand, revenue ranges, churn, cash runway, or a defined success score. They cannot know whether a startup will “succeed overall” with certainty. Predictions inherit the assumptions, missing information, and bias in their training data.

Research lab

R + LASSO

Test startup signals with data

The learning guides above help students make decisions today. This research lab asks a narrower question: which observed startup characteristics are associated with a defined Success Score?

Two models are prepared. The earlier-stage model uses age, country, industry, funding stage, total funding, and employee count. The all-observed model adds annual revenue and valuation. Because revenue and valuation may be consequences of success, the second model is descriptive rather than causal.

Research data needed: data/global_startup_success_dataset-selected-columns.csv contains the expected column names but no populated records. All 124 rows in the supplied file are blank. The learning platform and calculators work now; R graphs and model results will appear after the file is replaced with populated data.

Dataset overview

The dashboard begins with a basic data-quality check before showing any model results. Missing values, sample size, and category coverage matter because a clean-looking graph can still be misleading when the underlying sample is thin.

Factor comparisons

Pearson correlation measures linear association; Spearman correlation also detects monotonic relationships and is less sensitive to extreme values. Correlation does not establish that a factor causes startup success.

Country, industry, and funding-stage relationships

Group averages can be unstable for categories represented by few startups. Accordingly, each plot shows the group sample size and only displays the 12 largest groups.

LASSO regression

The data are split 80/20 into training and test sets. All imputation, dummy encoding, removal of zero-variance columns, and standardization are learned only from the training data. Cross-validation selects the penalty. The conservative lambda.1se value is used for the final model; it usually produces a smaller, more stable set of predictors than the minimum-error penalty.

Out-of-sample performance

A useful model should have RMSE below the mean-only baseline on held-out data. Negative test R-squared means the model generalized worse than simply predicting the test-set mean.

Selected factors

Because inputs are standardized, coefficient magnitudes are broadly comparable. A positive coefficient is associated with a higher predicted success score, holding the other included variables constant; a zero coefficient was excluded by LASSO. Category coefficients are relative to the omitted reference category.

Prediction check

Research conclusions

  • These results identify associations, not causal effects. Funding, hiring, revenue, valuation, and success may influence one another.
  • The startup name is excluded because it is an identifier, not a reusable explanatory factor.
  • LASSO may choose one variable from a group of highly correlated variables and shrink the others to zero. A zero coefficient does not prove that a factor is irrelevant.
  • Country and industry estimates need adequate representation. Results for small categories are unstable and should not drive decisions alone.
  • The held-out test metrics are the best guide to whether the relationships generalize beyond this sample.
  • A stronger causal analysis would require time-stamped predictors measured before the success outcome, a clear definition of Success Score, and preferably repeated observations over time.

Research methodology

The analysis uses an 80/20 training-test split. Preprocessing is learned from the training data only: missing numeric values are median-imputed, new and missing categories are handled explicitly, categorical variables are dummy encoded, and numeric predictors are standardized. Ten-fold cross-validation (or fewer folds for small samples) selects the LASSO penalty. The conservative one-standard-error penalty is reported to favor a simpler model.

The full R source is available in the project repository so every figure and metric can be rebuilt when the dataset changes.

Reproducibility details

The report was generated with R and records its complete package environment in the source build. This keeps the public page focused while preserving the technical details in the repository.
